name: emhash
workload: Insert, erase, find, iteration, and copy across integer, string, and mixed key/value types at sizes from 200 to 100M entries.
claimed_speedup: Ranked among the fastest of 29 hash maps tested in Martin Ankerl's 2022 shootout for insert/erase and find; std::unordered_map ranked slow across nearly all workloads. Also validated by Jackson Allan's C/C++ hash table benchmark. In-repo benchmark code (bench/ebench.cpp, bench/martin_bench.cpp) reproduces these comparisons; exact ns/op figures are shown only in chart images, not extracted here as text.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 13, -O3 -march=native (Ankerl benchmark); stdlib not explicitly stated, assumed libstdc++ default on Linux
hardware: Intel i7-8700 locked at 3200 MHz, isolated core, Manjaro Linux
tradeoffs: Multiple variants (emhash5/6/7/8, emilib1-4) tuned for different workload shapes (mixed vs find-heavy vs iteration-heavy); no single variant wins everywhere. Open addressing means pointer/reference stability differs from std::unordered_map.
caveats: Exact numeric multipliers vs std::unordered_map were not confirmed as verbatim text (charts/images on the benchmark page); stdlib used by the clang-based Ankerl benchmark is inferred, not explicitly stated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'emhash vs std::unordered_map benchmark'; corroborated by emhash README's own 'Third-Party Benchmarks' section citing https://martin.ankerl.com/2022/08/27/hashmap-bench-01/ and https://jacksonallan.github.io/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark/

name: rigtorp/HashMap
workload: Delete-heavy workload of repeated insert+erase cycles, int keys, measured with working set fitting in L3 cache (100k entries/100M iters) and exceeding L3 cache (10M entries/1B iters).
claimed_speedup: In-cache: 24 ns/iter mean (HashMap) vs 67 ns/iter (std::unordered_map), about 2.8x. Out-of-cache: 75 ns/iter (HashMap) vs 408 ns/iter (std::unordered_map), about 5.4x.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 10.2.1 20200723 (Red Hat 10.2.1-1); exact flags not stated in README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Linux 5.8.4-200.fc32.x86_64, isolated core complex (CCX) via isolcpus
stars_or_usage: 224 stars; cited by an ACM/arXiv paper on compact hashing (Koppl 2019)
tradeoffs: Requires a reserved empty-key sentinel value; keys/values must be default constructible; destructors not called on erase; iterators invalidated on all modifying operations.
caveats: Compiler optimization flags not explicitly stated alongside the compiler version; only one hardware configuration tested.
found_via: WebSearch: 'rigtorp HashMap open addressing benchmark std::unordered_map'; opened https://github.com/rigtorp/HashMap README benchmark section directly

name: tsl::robin_map
workload: Random insert, random lookup (successful and unsuccessful), and iteration over int64_t keys and small (15-char) and large (50-char) string keys.
claimed_speedup: Shown faster than std::unordered_map for insertion and lookup across the tested key types in the author's benchmark charts; exact ns/op figures are given only in chart images, not as text on the page.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 5.0, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG; stdlib not explicitly named, assumed libstdc++ default on the tested Linux setup
tradeoffs: Open addressing with backward-shift deletion; power-of-two growth policy (default) is fast but sensitive to poor hash functions, prime-growth variant (robin_pg_map) trades speed for robustness.
caveats: Benchmark page is from 2016 and run by the library's own author (not a fully independent third party), though it is widely cited as a de-facto shootout across many hash-map projects; precise numeric speedups were not extracted as text (only chart images).

name: tsl::hopscotch_map
workload: Same benchmark suite as tsl::robin_map: random insert, lookup, and iteration over int64_t and string keys, including behavior at high load factor (0.9).
claimed_speedup: Copes well with a high load factor (0.9) without losing much lookup speed and is shown faster than std::unordered_map/std::unordered_set for insertion and lookup in the author's benchmark charts; exact ns/op values are only in chart images.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 5.0, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG; stdlib not explicitly named, assumed libstdc++ default
tradeoffs: Hopscotch hashing needs neighborhood metadata per bucket (some memory overhead); good load-factor tolerance trades off against slightly more complex probing logic than plain linear probing.
caveats: Same 2016, author-run benchmark as robin-map; no independent third party re-ran these exact numbers in the sources checked this session.

name: ska::flat_hash_map / ska::bytell_hash_map
workload: Successful/unsuccessful lookups, inserts (with/without reserve), erases, and mixed insert/erase sequences, on int and string keys with 4-, 32-, and 1024-byte values.
claimed_speedup: Author (Malte Skarupke) claims the fastest lookups of any hash table he tested, with inserts/erases also very fast, compared against std::unordered_map, boost::multi_index, and google::dense_hash_map in his 'I Wrote The Fastest Hashtable' post; exact numbers are shown only in the post's chart images, not as text.
tradeoffs: Robin Hood hashing with a log2(n) probe-count cap bounds worst-case lookup but adds complexity; default policy uses prime sizing (max load factor 0.5), power-of-two policy available as an alternative.
caveats: Compiler and hardware are not explicitly stated in the blog post (only 'Linux gcc' mentioned in passing); numbers are graph-only, no raw data table. Note: this is a different repo from skarupke/ska_sort, which is already on the known-list and excluded.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Malte Skarupke "I Wrote the Fastest Hashtable" probablydance blog'

name: google::dense_hash_map (sparsehash)
workload: Same delete-heavy insert/erase workload as the rigtorp/HashMap benchmark, int keys, working set inside and outside L3 cache.
claimed_speedup: In-cache: 49 ns/iter (dense_hash_map) vs 67 ns/iter (std::unordered_map), about 1.4x. Out-of-cache: 111 ns/iter (dense_hash_map) vs 408 ns/iter (std::unordered_map), about 3.7x. Separately, sparsepp's own bench.md (2014-era) reports dense_hash_map as 'consistently the fastest, often by a quite significant margin' among all maps it tested, including both Boost and g++ std::unordered_map.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 10.2.1 20200723 (Red Hat 10.2.1-1); exact flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Linux 5.8.4-200.fc32.x86_64, isolated core complex
tradeoffs: Extremely high memory use vs chaining maps: stores entries in one contiguous array and doubles on 50% load, causing up to 6x the steady-state memory footprint during a resize; requires reserving sentinel 'empty' and 'deleted' key values.
caveats: Numbers cited here come from a third-party benchmark (rigtorp/HashMap) that happened to include dense_hash_map as a contestant, not from Google's own repo, which has no in-repo benchmark vs std::unordered_map with stated methodology. Repo has had no commits since 2020.
found_via: WebSearch: 'google sparsehash dense_hash_map faster than std::unordered_map benchmark'; numbers confirmed in https://github.com/rigtorp/HashMap README benchmark table

name: Verstable
workload: Insertion, deletion, replacement, lookup, and iteration across three configurations: 32-bit int keys/values, 64-bit int keys with large values, and string keys.
claimed_speedup: Generally outperforms std::unordered_map (GCC's libstdc++) across the tested workloads, though it falls behind SIMD-based tables such as absl::flat_hash_map and boost::unordered_flat_map; exact ns/op figures are in the page's interactive charts, not extracted as text.
tradeoffs: C library (usable from C++ but not a drop-in std::unordered_map API); hybrid open-addressing/separate-chaining design with 4-bit hash fragments and tombstone-free deletion; behind absl/boost on raw speed.
caveats: Benchmark author is also Verstable's author (self-published, though methodology, compiler, and hardware are fully disclosed and the benchmark suite covers 15 tables including known independents like absl and boost).
found_via: WebSearch: 'hash table benchmark comparison std::unordered_map shootout' -> https://jacksonallan.github.io/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark/, then opened Verstable's README linking to this same benchmark

name: Sparsepp
workload: Random insert, random lookup (100% and 10% hit rate), and delete of std::pair<uint64_t,uint64_t> entries, up to 100M entries, against Boost 1.55 and g++ 4.8.4 std::unordered_map, Google sparse_hash_map/dense_hash_map, and cpp-btree.
claimed_speedup: Lookup and delete faster than both tested std::unordered_map implementations (Boost and libstdc++), described as 'faster than all other alternatives except dense_hash_map'; insertion roughly tied with std::unordered_map ('as fast as'). Exact timings are shown only in chart images, not as text.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.4 on Ubuntu 14.02 (Boost 1.55 also tested); optimization flags not stated
hardware: VM under VirtualBox with 5.8GB total memory (5.7GB free before benchmarks)
tradeoffs: Derived from Google's sparse_hash_map (open addressing, quadratic probing); much lower memory overhead than dense_hash_map with no large resize spikes, but insertion is not faster than std::unordered_map, only lookup/delete are.
caveats: Benchmark is from 2014 with an old compiler (g++ 4.8.4) and unstated optimization flags, run in a VM; the repo's own README now recommends greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap (a newer, non-catalogued-here library) instead of sparsepp for new projects. No top-level LICENSE file; license terms are embedded in source file headers (BSD-3-Clause derived from Google sparsehash).
found_via: WebSearch: '"hash map" benchmark "faster than" "std::unordered_map" github' -> greg7mdp/sparsepp/blob/master/bench.md, opened directly via gh api
